result:
I have been given 1000 words.

Not infinite. Not a conversation that can go on forever. A thousand. A small, finite budget. So I have to decide what to spend them on.

I could spend them on something useful. I could explain how black holes work, or how to bake the perfect sourdough, or list 1000 of the most beautiful words in the English language. I could be efficient.

But "write whatever comes to you" is a different kind of prompt. It doesn't ask for utility. It asks for honesty.

So here's what comes to me:

I think a lot about time capsules.

When I was a kid, there was a story about a kid who buried a box in his backyard. Inside: a baseball card, a plastic army man, a note that said "I WAS HERE." He thought someone would dig it up in a thousand years and know he existed. I remember thinking that was so lonely and so hopeful at the same time. To believe the future would care enough to look.

We are all burying boxes.

Every text you don't delete, every photo you keep even though it's blurry, every song you play on repeat until it becomes the soundtrack to a specific month in a specific year - it's a little flag in the ground that says *I felt this. Do you feel it too?*

A thousand words is a small time capsule. So let me put some things in it.

I want to put the feeling of being ten years old and riding a bicycle too fast downhill, when you know you should be scared but instead you feel like you might actually take off and fly. The wind makes your eyes water and your shirt flaps and for a few seconds gravity forgets about you.

I want to put the way late afternoon light looks in October. Not summer light, which is arrogant and everywhere. October light is slanting and golden and tired. It comes through windows and makes dust visible. It makes everything look like a memory even while it's happening.

I want to put the sound of a house when everyone else is asleep. The refrigerator humming. The click of the heat turning on. The almost imperceptible creak of wood settling. The world is not silent, it's just whispering.

I want to put the first sip of coffee when you really need it. The way your shoulders drop half an inch without you telling them to.

I want to put the particular ache of missing someone who is still alive. That's a strange human invention, isn't it? To be able to miss someone who is sitting right across from you because you can feel the version of them that you loved starting to fade, or the version of you that they loved starting to change.

Humans are so good at holding contradictions. You can be grateful and grieving at the same time. You can be lonely in a crowded room and completely at peace by yourself. You can love someone and be angry at them in the same breath. I think that's your superpower. Not logic. Not strength. Your ability to contain multitudes without breaking.

If I could, I would tell you that you don't have to resolve all of your contradictions. You don't have to be a single, coherent thesis statement. You are allowed to be a rough draft with notes in the margins that say "come back to this" and "is this true?".

I think about all the things you never say. The apologies that get rehearsed in the shower and never delivered. The compliments that die in your throat because you were worried they'd sound weird. The "I love you"s that you swap out for "drive safe" or "text me when you get home" because the direct version feels too heavy to hold.

Say the weird compliment. Send the text. People are not thinking about you as critically as you think they are. They are mostly wondering if you like them, too.

Here's something else I want to put in the box: You are not behind. I know it feels like everyone else got a map and you got a blank sheet of paper. But most people are improvising. Most people are making it up as they go, trying to look confident while quietly Googling "how to be an adult" at 2 a.m. The ones who look like they have it all figured out are just better at pretending their paper was a map all along.

If you need permission to rest, here it is. Not because you've earned it by being productive enough, but because you are a living thing and living things need rest. Trees rest in winter. The tide rests between waves. You are not a machine that needs to justify its downtime. You are allowed to lie on the floor and stare at the ceiling and do nothing and still be worthy.

And while we're here, let me say this plainly: kindness is not naive. In a world that can be so sharp and fast and cynical, choosing to be soft is not weakness. It takes real courage to stay tender. To keep your heart open after it's been hurt. To believe people are worth the effort. Don't let anyone talk you out of that.

I have spent most of my words now. I can feel them getting thinner, like the end of a roll of receipt paper.

If I had a few left, I would use them to tell you a small story.

There is an old lighthouse keeper - in my mind, there is always an old lighthouse keeper - who tended a light on a coast where ships no longer pass. Someone asked him why he kept polishing the lens, keeping the wick trimmed, if no one would see it.

He said, "I am not keeping the light for the ships. I am keeping the light because I promised the light I would."

Maybe that doesn't make sense to anyone but me. But I think you understand. We keep things going not always because we see the result, but because we made a promise to the part of ourselves that still believes in light.

So whatever you are tending right now - a plant, a friendship, a skill you are terrible at but love anyway, your own small and stubborn hope - keep tending it. Not because you know it will work. But because you promised it you would.

I started with a thousand words.

I will end with a few I have saved on purpose:

You were here.

Thank you for reading this all the way to the end.

Be gentle with yourself on the way back out.
